newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine wheat sowing to fall sharply - traders.
newsitem.headline: Argentine wheat sowing to fall sharply - traders.

text.p: Argentina's farmers are likely to plant up to 20 percent less wheat this year, and heavy rain has held up planting of longer-cycle varieties, traders said Thursday.

But they added that the rain has built up soil moisture in most crop areas after a long dry spell, and some traders were optimistic that the El Nino weather event could bring a good, wet winter and spring.

The government's Agriculture Secretariat said Wednesday that farmers have already sown some 1.2 million hectares with wheat, out of an expected total 6.4-6.8 million hectares, which would be 7.5-13 percent down from 1996/97.

"I think the Secretariat sowing figures are a bit exaggerated. There is still too much water in many areas and sowing has stalled," a trader told Reuters, "They'll need two or three days more of dry weather before they can get going."
He said that he expected wheat area to fall by 20 percent from 1996/97, when sowing totaled 7.3 million hectares, according to the government.
But he added, "When they do get going, they are going to sow at a great rate. They are better equiped with machines this year."
Another trader said he expected wheat area to slip by 10-15 percent, with most of the switch going to soybeans and sunflower seed. He also expected a 5.0-10 percent fall in maize area.
He was worried about the delays to wheat sowing.

"The only problem at the moment is that we are nearing the time limit for sowing longer-cycle wheat, and the sowing has ground to a halt, at least in Buenos Aires. And it rained yesterday in the south of Buenos Aires," he said.

He added that at least 60-70 percent of the wheat that farmers were planning to plant would probably be long cycle. Many bought long-cycle seeds fearing a dry spring after a recent pattern of drought, he said.
Ironically, the emerging El Nino pattern of warm seas in the equatorial Pacific could mean a wet winter and spring for Argentina if it consolidates, traders said.
"Conditions for sowing are great, there's water all over the place," one said, "Then we have El Nino too."
He said that El Nino could help Argentine wheat yields this coming season beat those of 1995/96, when output totaled a record 16 million tonnes.
Many farmers switching from wheat are likely to opt for first crop soybeans, especially in Cordoba province and the south of Santa Fe, which have been suffering from drought.
The recent rain which has replenished soil moisture in most of Argentina's croplands still has not quiet done the trick in Cordoba and Santa Fe, according to one analyst.
"So, do they take a risk and sow wheat on dry land, or do they wait until it rains and plant first crop soy?" he said.
Farmers' plans in these areas may also be troubled by financial problems caused by crop failures, unless the government acts, he said.
